title: The LORD's Anointed King on Zion
summary: The nations and their rulers conspire against the LORD and his Anointed One, resolving to throw off his rule. God in heaven laughs at them and announces that he has installed his King on Zion. The king then reports the LORD's decree, “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father,” with the nations promised as his inheritance. The psalm ends by urging the kings of the earth to serve the LORD with fear and to kiss the Son, and it closes with a blessing on all who take refuge in him.
story:
Psalm 2 is the second half of the Psalter's gateway. Psalm 1 pictures the person rooted in God's instruction; Psalm 2 turns to the nations and to the king God has chosen. Neither psalm has a heading, unlike nearly every other psalm in Book I (Psalms 1 to 41), and the two are bound together by a frame: Psalm 1 opens with “Blessed is the man”, and Psalm 2 closes with “Blessed are all who take refuge in Him.” The Babylonian Talmud (Berakhot 9b-10a) treats them as a single psalm, and Codex Bezae, a fifth-century manuscript of Acts, has Paul cite Psalm 2:7 from ‘the first psalm’ (Acts 13:33). Read together, they announce the two great subjects of the whole book: a life shaped by God's word, and God's reign through his anointed king.

Behind the psalm stands God's covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7, where God promised David a descendant whose throne would last forever and said, “I will be his Father, and he will be My son” (2 Samuel 7:14). Psalm 2 turns that promise into a coronation decree. The Psalter then follows the promise through hard history. Psalm 3 begins with David fleeing from his own son Absalom, so the confident king of Psalm 2 is at once a hunted man. Royal psalms stand at turning points along the way: Psalm 72 closes Book II with a prayer that the king will rule to the ends of the earth, and Psalm 89 closes Book III with a lament that God has renounced the covenant with his servant and cast his throne to the ground. By the time the book is finished, the promise of Psalm 2 has become a hope waiting for its king. The New Testament opens by announcing him, and it quotes this psalm from the baptism of Jesus to the last battle in Revelation.
historical:
Psalm 2 is a royal psalm, one of the group that Hermann Gunkel identified in his form-critical study of the Psalter (completed after his death by Joachim Begrich and published in 1933) as poems about Israel's king: Psalms 2, 18, 20, 21, 45, 72, 89, 101, 110, 132, and 144:1-11. It has no heading, though the earliest church attributed it to David (Acts 4:25). Most scholars place its composition during the monarchy in Jerusalem (roughly 1000 to 586 BC) and read it as part of a coronation liturgy, spoken when a son of David was installed or when his installation was remembered. Sigmund Mowinckel (Psalmenstudien, 1921 to 1924) connected the royal psalms with an annual autumn festival at which the LORD's kingship and the king's were celebrated together; Peter Craigie (Psalms 1-50, Word Biblical Commentary, 1983) and others prefer the simpler setting of a coronation. A few have dated the psalm much later. Marco Treves (Vetus Testamentum, 1965) claimed to find an acrostic in it naming the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus (reigned 103 to 76 BC), but the proposal requires reading selected letters and has found little support.

The situation the psalm describes was a real danger in the ancient world. The death of a king and the accession of his heir was the moment subject peoples chose to test the new ruler. When Ahab died, Moab rebelled against Israel (2 Kings 1:1; 3:5), a revolt the Moabite king Mesha celebrated in his own inscription, the Mesha Stele (about 840 BC). When the Assyrian king Sargon II died in 705 BC, Hezekiah of Judah joined a wave of rebellions, which brought Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC (2 Kings 18:7, 13). Assyrian kings tried to prevent such revolts by binding their subjects with oaths in advance. In 672 BC Esarhaddon made officials and vassals swear loyalty to his chosen heir, Ashurbanipal, and copies of this Succession Treaty have been excavated at Nimrud and, in 2009, at Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey. Psalm 2 answers the same danger in a different way: not with a treaty imposed by the king, but with a decree spoken by God.

After 586 BC no son of David reigned in Jerusalem, and the psalm could no longer describe the present. Its place at the head of the Psalter suggests that the editors of the book read it as a promise still open, and later Jewish writings show how it was heard. The Psalms of Solomon, written after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, pray for a son of David who will shatter the arrogance of sinners like a potter's jar and break their substance with an iron rod (Psalms of Solomon 17:23-24), borrowing the words of verse 9. At Qumran the Florilegium (4Q174) quotes verses 1 and 2 and applies them to the nations raging against the elect of Israel at the end of days, beside a reading of 2 Samuel 7 that expects the Branch of David. The Rule of the Congregation (1QSa 2:11-12) may speak of the time when God begets the Messiah, an echo of verse 7, but the key letter is damaged and some scholars read ‘leads’ instead of ‘begets’. The Babylonian Talmud (Sukkah 52a) applies verses 7 and 8 to the Messiah son of David, to whom God says ‘ask of me’.
cultural:
Several images come from the ceremony of kingship. Kings in Israel were anointed with oil at their installation (1 Samuel 16:13; 1 Kings 1:39), which is why the king is called the LORD's anointed, mashiach. When the boy Joash was made king, the priest Jehoiada put the crown on him and gave him ‘the testimony’ before he was anointed (2 Kings 11:12). Gerhard von Rad (in a 1947 essay on the royal ritual in Judah) compared this with the Egyptian royal protocol, a document in which a god gave the new pharaoh his throne names and acknowledged him as the god's son, and he argued that the decree of verse 7 is Judah's counterpart: a written charter, read out by the king, that declares his sonship. Many scholars accept the comparison in general while doubting that Judah borrowed the Egyptian rite directly.

The language of sonship needs care. In Egypt the pharaoh was called son of the sun god Re in his official titles and was treated as divine. Israel's texts speak differently. The decree says “today I have become Your Father”: the relationship begins on a particular day, the day of enthronement, which is the language of adoption, not of physical descent or divine nature. The same covenant idea appears in Psalm 89, where God promises of David, “I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth” (Psalm 89:27). The king is God's son as the one who represents God's rule on earth and receives the family inheritance, which in this psalm is the whole world. Nachalah (inheritance) and achuzzah (possession) in verse 8 are the legal words for family land in Israel, now stretched to “the ends of the earth”.

Zion was the fortified ridge David captured from the Jebusites (2 Samuel 5:7), where he brought the ark and where Solomon built the temple, so ‘My holy mountain’ joins the king's throne to God's dwelling. The iron rod of verse 9 is a shevet, the same word for a shepherd's club and a king's scepter (Genesis 49:10), made of iron to show it cannot be broken. Smashing pottery was a known picture of total defeat. In Egypt during the Middle Kingdom (about 2000 to 1700 BC) scribes wrote the names of hostile rulers and peoples on bowls and clay figurines and then broke them in a ritual of cursing; scholars call these the Execration Texts, and some of them appear to name Jerusalem. A potter's jar, once shattered, cannot be mended (Jeremiah 19:11).

The ending uses the language of treaty and court. To serve (avad) is what a vassal does for his overlord as well as what a worshiper does for God. To kiss was a gesture of homage: Samuel kisses Saul at his anointing (1 Samuel 10:1), and worshipers of Baal kissed their idol (1 Kings 19:18; Hosea 13:2). On the Black Obelisk of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III (about 825 BC) Jehu of Israel, or his envoy, is shown prostrate before the king. The rebels of verse 3 are offered terms before judgment falls, as ancient kings offered rebellious vassals a chance to return to loyalty.
literary:
The psalm has four stanzas of three verses each, and each has its own speaker and scene. Verses 1 to 3 are on earth: the psalmist asks why the nations rage, and then the rulers speak their own words, “Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords.” Verses 4 to 6 move to heaven, where the one enthroned laughs and then speaks: “I have installed My King on Zion.” Verses 7 to 9 give the king's own voice, reporting the decree God spoke to him. Verses 10 to 12 return to earth with a direct appeal to the kings, most naturally in the voice of the psalmist or the king. The movement is earth, heaven, king, earth, and the logic is that of a trial: the charge (rebellion), the verdict (the king is installed), the legal basis (the decree), and the sentence offered with mercy (be wise, serve, kiss, take refuge).

The stanzas answer each other in sound and word. The rebels say ‘let us’ twice (verse 3, a pair of cohortatives), and God answers with an emphatic ‘I’ (verse 6: ‘but I, I have installed’). The poetic suffix -emo, ‘their’ or ‘them’, runs through verses 3 to 5, tying the rebels' words to God's reply. The rebels speak; God speaks back (verse 5); the king recounts what God spoke (verse 7). The earth is named at both ends: ‘the kings of the earth’ in verse 2 and “the ends of the earth” and ‘judges of the earth’ in verses 8 and 10.

The strongest literary links are with Psalm 1. The verb hagah, used of the righteous man who meditates on God's law day and night (Psalm 1:2), is the verb for the peoples who ‘plot’ in verse 1: the same activity of murmuring over words, turned to opposite ends. Psalm 1 ends with “the way of the wicked will perish” (Psalm 1:6), and Psalm 2:12 warns the kings that they will perish in the way (derekh, ‘way’, and avad, ‘perish’, in both). The ‘blessed’ that opens Psalm 1 returns as the last word of blessing in Psalm 2. The editors who placed these psalms together framed the whole Psalter with a single choice between two ways, and between two kinds of kings.

outline.t: The nations conspire against the LORD and his Anointed
God laughs and installs his King on Zion
The decree: You are my Son
A warning to the kings: serve the LORD and kiss the Son

doctrines.note: The psalm names the king God installs on Zion his Anointed One (mashiach, the source of Messiah and, through the Greek christos, of Christ) and his Son. It is the Old Testament text that joins the three titles the Gospels give Jesus: Christ, Son of God, and King (compare John 1:49). After the monarchy fell it became one of the foundational texts of Jewish hope for a coming son of David.

Verse 6 speaks of a king installed by God on his holy mountain, and verse 7 of a decree spoken on the day of enthronement. The apostles read that day as the resurrection and ascension: Paul applies verse 7 to God raising Jesus (Acts 13:33), and Hebrews uses it for the Son's appointment above the angels and as high priest (Hebrews 1:5; 5:5).

God's rule is exercised through his chosen king, and the inheritance promised to him is not one nation but “the ends of the earth” (verse 8). Human revolt against that rule is real but ‘in vain’ (verse 1), and the kingdom's final extent is universal. Revelation takes up the iron rod of verse 9 for Christ's reign over the nations.

The LORD rebukes the rebels in anger (verse 5), the king breaks them like pottery (verse 9), and his wrath can ignite “in an instant” (verse 12). Yet judgment is announced before it falls, with a call to wisdom and submission (verses 10 and 11), so that the warning itself is an act of mercy.

The last line turns from threat to promise: “Blessed are all who take refuge in Him.” The verb chasah, ‘take refuge’, is one of the Psalter's words for trust, and the psalm makes clear that the only safe place from the king's anger is the king himself.

words.note: Mashiach, anointed one. It occurs about thirty-nine times in the Hebrew Bible, ten of them in the Psalms, and most often means the king anointed with oil for his office (‘the LORD's anointed’, 1 Samuel 24:6); it is also used of the anointed priest (Leviticus 4:3) and once of the Persian Cyrus as God's chosen instrument (Isaiah 45:1). The standard lexicons treat it as a title of office, not yet a technical term for a future savior. Psalm 2, placed at the head of the Psalter, is one of the places where the word began to gather that future sense, which is why Messiah (from Hebrew) and Christ (from the Greek christos) both come from it.

Hagah, to murmur, mutter, meditate, or plot. It occurs about twenty-five times, half of them in the Psalms. The verb describes a low sound: a dove's moaning (Isaiah 38:14), a lion growling over its prey (Isaiah 31:4), a person reading under the breath. In Psalm 1:2 the righteous man ‘meditates’ on God's law day and night; in verse 1 here the peoples ‘plot’ in vain. The same act of murmuring over words can be devotion or conspiracy, and the pairing is one sign that the two psalms were read as one.

Choq, decree, statute, fixed portion. The noun comes from a root meaning to inscribe or engrave, and it is a common word in the law for God's statutes (Deuteronomy 4:1, where it stands beside mishpatim, rules). In verse 7 the king recounts ‘the decree of the LORD’, a formal and binding declaration, which many scholars connect with the written ‘testimony’ given to Joash at his coronation (2 Kings 11:12). The word stresses that the king's sonship rests on God's word, not on the king's claim.

Yalad, to bear or beget, one of the commonest verbs in the Hebrew Bible (nearly five hundred times), used both of a mother giving birth and of a father fathering a child. In verse 7 the perfect yelidtikha, ‘I have begotten you’, is joined to hayyom, ‘today’, and the combination signals a legal act rather than a biological one: on the day of enthronement God declares the king his son. The BSB's “today I have become Your Father” renders that sense. Christian theology later distinguished this royal begetting from the Son's eternal generation (see the hard questions below).

Nachalah, inheritance, the property that passes within a family. It occurs over two hundred times and is the key word for each tribe's allotted land in Joshua and for Israel as God's own inheritance (Deuteronomy 32:9). In verse 8 God offers his son an inheritance that is not a share of Canaan but the nations themselves, with achuzzah, ‘possession’, in parallel. The promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3) here becomes a promise that the earth will belong to David's greater son.

Nashaq, to kiss, about thirty times in the Hebrew Bible, used of family affection (Genesis 29:11), of reconciliation (Genesis 33:4), of the homage paid to a king (1 Samuel 10:1), and of devotion to an idol (1 Kings 19:18). Here it is a Piel imperative addressed to rulers, calling for a public act of submission and loyalty. What they are to kiss is the most debated question in the psalm (see the text note and the first hard question).

Chasah, to seek refuge, take shelter. It occurs about thirty-seven times, twenty-five of them in the Psalms, where it is one of the chief words for trust in God (Psalm 5:11; 7:1; 11:1; 18:2; 57:1). The picture is of a person running under a rock, a wall, or a bird's wings for protection. The final line of Psalm 2 uses the participle, “all who take refuge in him”, and whether ‘him’ is the LORD or the Son, the refuge from the king's anger is found in coming to the king.

christ:
The New Testament quotes and echoes Psalm 2 more often than almost any other psalm, and only Psalm 110 rivals it among the royal psalms. It does so because the psalm joins the titles the first Christians confessed of Jesus: the LORD's Anointed, his Son, and the King enthroned on Zion.

When Peter and John were threatened by the council in Jerusalem, the church prayed verses 1 and 2 and applied them to the conspiracy against Jesus: “Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel against Your holy servant Jesus, whom You anointed” (Acts 4:27). The reading is striking in its scope. The rebels of the psalm are not only foreign nations but every group that joined in rejecting the Anointed, Jewish and Gentile alike, and the church sees the psalm fulfilled in the cross before it sees it fulfilled in any triumph.

The decree of verse 7 is read in three ways. At Jesus' baptism the voice from heaven says, “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11), joining the first words of the decree to the servant language of Isaiah 42:1, and at the transfiguration the voice repeats the declaration (Mark 9:7). Paul, preaching at Pisidian Antioch, applies ‘today’ to the resurrection: God has fulfilled his promise “by raising up Jesus. As it is written in the second Psalm” (Acts 13:33); compare Romans 1:4, where Jesus is declared Son of God with power by his resurrection. Hebrews uses the verse to show that the Son is greater than the angels (Hebrews 1:5, beside 2 Samuel 7:14) and that Christ did not appoint himself high priest but was appointed by the one who called him Son (Hebrews 5:5). The enthronement day of the psalm becomes Easter and the ascension, when the crucified Messiah takes his throne.

Revelation takes up verses 8 and 9. The risen Christ promises the faithful in Thyatira that they will share his authority: “He will rule them with an iron scepter and shatter them like pottery” (Revelation 2:27), an authority he has himself received from his Father. The male child of Revelation 12:5 will rule the nations with an iron scepter, and in 19:15 the rider on the white horse does so. Revelation follows the Septuagint, which reads ‘shepherd’ where the Hebrew has ‘break’, so the iron rod is at once a shepherd's staff and a weapon of judgment.

The link is not only thematic. The psalm was first a coronation text for kings of David's line, and none of those kings received the ends of the earth. The New Testament's claim is that the promise always outran the kings who first heard it and finally met its match in Jesus, the Son of David who is also the Son of God. The final line keeps the gospel's shape: the one who will judge the nations is the refuge of all who come to him.
interpretation:
Jewish readers applied the psalm both to David and to the Messiah. The Babylonian Talmud reads it messianically in two places: in Sukkah 52a God says to the Messiah son of David ‘ask of me’ (verse 8), and in Avodah Zarah 3b God's laughter (verse 4) is his response to the final revolt of Gog and Magog. Berakhot 9b-10a counts Psalms 1 and 2 as one psalm. In eleventh-century France Rashi noted that the rabbis had expounded the psalm of the King Messiah, but argued that its plain sense, and the right answer to the minim (sectarians, here Christians), was to read it of David and the nations who gathered against him after his anointing (2 Samuel 5:17). Abraham ibn Ezra, in twelfth-century Spain, took the difficult bar of verse 12 as ‘son’, citing Proverbs 31:2, and applied the psalm to the anointed king, whether David or the Messiah.

Christian writers took the psalm as prophecy of Christ from the beginning. Justin Martyr (First Apology 40, around 155) quotes Psalms 1 and 2 together as a single prophecy, and in his Dialogue with Trypho (chapters 88 and 103) he gives the words at Jesus' baptism as the whole of verse 7, the reading also found in Codex Bezae at Luke 3:22. Augustine's Expositions of the Psalms read ‘today’ as the eternal present of God, in which nothing is past or future, and so as the Son's eternal generation. Theodore of Mopsuestia (died 428), the leading Antiochene interpreter, read most psalms against the history of Israel but counted Psalm 2 among only four psalms (with 8, 45, and 110) that speak directly of Christ. Jerome's translation from the Hebrew rendered verse 12 ‘worship purely’ (adorate pure), though he defended ‘son’ as a possible meaning.

Calvin's commentary on the Psalms (1557) read the psalm first of David and his kingdom, as a type in which Christ's kingdom was foreshadowed, and he explained the begetting of verse 7 as the day when the king's sonship was made known. Modern critical study since Gunkel and Mowinckel has read it as a royal coronation psalm, and Gerhard von Rad (1947) compared the decree with Egyptian royal protocols. Gerald Wilson's The Editing of the Hebrew Psalter (1985) turned attention to the psalm's place in the book, showing how royal psalms stand at the seams between its books (2, 72, 89) and trace the rise and apparent collapse of David's line. Adela Yarbro Collins and John J. Collins (King and Messiah as Son of God, 2008) trace the idea of the king as God's son from the ancient Near East through Psalm 2 to the New Testament.

In worship the psalm has a long life. Verse 7 is the introit of the Midnight Mass of Christmas in the Roman rite, Dominus dixit ad me, ‘The Lord said to me, You are my Son, today I have begotten you’, sung to the Gregorian chant. The Revised Common Lectionary appoints Psalm 2 (or Psalm 99) for Transfiguration Sunday in Year A. Handel's Messiah (1742) builds the climax of Part Two from the psalm: an aria on the raging nations, a chorus on breaking their bonds, a recitative on the one who dwells in heaven laughing them to scorn, and a tenor aria on breaking them with a rod of iron, which leads directly into the Hallelujah chorus.
text:
Psalm 2 has the same number in Hebrew, Greek, and English Bibles, and no heading to shift the verse numbers. The differences between English Bibles come from a few hard words and from the ancient translations.

In verse 6 the Masoretic Text has God speaking, ‘I have installed my king’. The Septuagint reads the same consonants with different vowels and a different person, ‘I was appointed king by him on Zion’, making the king the speaker from verse 6 onward. English Bibles follow the Hebrew. In verse 9 the Hebrew verb teroem, ‘you will break them’, can be read with other vowels as ‘you will shepherd them’, and the Septuagint took it that way (poimaneis). The New Testament quotations in Revelation 2:27, 12:5, and 19:15 follow the Greek, which is why an English reader meets ‘rule’ there where Psalm 2:9 has ‘break’.

Verses 11 and 12 are the real difficulty. The Hebrew reads ‘serve the LORD with fear, rejoice with trembling, kiss bar’. Bar is the ordinary Aramaic word for son (as in bar mitzvah), but the Hebrew word for son, used in verse 7, is ben; bar appears as Hebrew for son only in Proverbs 31:2, and in Hebrew the same letters can mean ‘pure’ or ‘grain’. The ancient versions divide. The Septuagint reads ‘take hold of instruction’ and the Aramaic Targum ‘receive instruction’; the Syriac Peshitta reads ‘kiss the son’; the second-century Jewish Greek translators Aquila and Symmachus took bar as ‘pure’ or ‘choice’, and Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew has ‘worship purely’. In the early twentieth century Alfred Bertholet proposed rearranging the letters of the last words of verse 11 and the first of verse 12 to read ‘with trembling kiss his feet’, and the NRSV adopts that conjecture, as did commentators such as Hans-Joachim Kraus. English versions therefore range from ‘kiss the Son’ (KJV, ESV, BSB) and ‘pay homage to the Son’ (CSB) to ‘kiss his feet’ (NRSV) and ‘pay homage in good faith’ (NJPS, which notes that the meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain). Whichever is right, the verse calls rulers to an act of homage.

teach.big: The nations' revolt against God's rule is noisy but empty, because God has already installed his Son as King, and the only safe place from the King's judgment is refuge in the King himself.

outline.t: Human power, at its most organized, treats God's rule as chains to be broken; the psalm names that revolt and calls it vain before a word of judgment is spoken.
Heaven is not anxious. God's laughter measures the gap between the rebels' plans and his throne, and his answer is not a counterattack but a King already installed.
The King's authority rests on God's decree and sonship, not on his own claim, and his inheritance is the whole earth; the New Testament hears this fulfilled in the risen Jesus.
Before judgment falls the rebels are offered terms: wisdom, reverent service, homage to the Son, and blessing for all who take refuge in him.

teach.pitfalls:
The most dangerous misreading turns the psalm into a charter for a nation or party. The kings of the earth in this psalm are all rulers, including Israel's (Acts 4:27 lists “the people of Israel” among them), and the only king it enthrones is God's anointed. Preaching that casts ‘the nations’ as the other side of a modern political contest, with the preacher's side as the anointed, repeats the very rebellion the psalm condemns. A second misreading takes verse 8, “Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance,” as a promise that any believer who asks boldly will receive power or wealth. The promise is addressed to the King, and believers share in it only as they share in his suffering and reign (Revelation 2:26-27).

Teachers should also avoid treating God's laughter in verse 4 as cruelty or as indifference to suffering; it is the laughter of sovereignty at the pretensions of power, the same scorn the psalm invites the oppressed to share. Do not build the doctrine of the Son's eternal generation on the word ‘today’ alone, since the New Testament applies it to the resurrection and the church's doctrine rests on wider ground. And do not preach the psalm only as threat. The last line is an invitation, and the call to ‘kiss the Son’ is offered to the very rulers who were plotting.
teach.pastoral: The psalm speaks to people who feel small before powers that seem unstoppable: the believer under a hostile government, the worker crushed by an institution, the family facing a system that does not care. It tells them that heaven is not anxious. It also speaks to people who have been harmed by leaders who used God's name to justify their own rule, including abusive pastors and parents. Teach clearly that the psalm gives no human authority the Son's place, and that the King it enthrones is the one who welcomes refugees.

hard.q: What does “Kiss the Son” mean in verse 12, and is it the right translation?
hard.a:
The strongest objection to the traditional rendering is linguistic and comes from Jewish and critical scholars alike. The word for son in verse 7 is the Hebrew ben; in verse 12 the text has bar, which is the Aramaic word for son and appears in Hebrew with that sense only in Proverbs 31:2. Why would a Hebrew poem switch to Aramaic for the same person? The earliest Jewish translations did not read ‘son’: the Septuagint has ‘take hold of instruction’, the Targum ‘receive instruction’, and Aquila and Symmachus ‘pure’ or ‘choice’. Medieval Jewish interpreters, with polemic against Christian readings in view, generally took bar as ‘purity’ or ‘grain’, and the Jewish Publication Society's translation (NJPS) renders the line ‘pay homage in good faith’. Many modern critical scholars, following Alfred Bertholet, think the text has been disturbed and rearrange the letters to read ‘kiss his feet’, as in the NRSV, arguing that the result gives two balanced lines and fits the ancient gesture of submission.

The case for ‘son’ is also substantial. Abraham ibn Ezra, a Jewish interpreter with no Christian motive, read bar as ‘son’ and pointed to Proverbs 31:2, and the Syriac Peshitta reads ‘kiss the son’. Defenders of the rendering, such as Peter Craigie in his Word Biblical Commentary (1983), argue that an Aramaic word addressed to foreign kings, who would have known Aramaic as the diplomatic language of the Near East, suits the speech, and that the verse naturally returns to the Son of verse 7, since the psalm has spoken of no other son. Others note that Bertholet's rearrangement requires changing the order of four words with no manuscript support, and that ‘kiss purely’ or ‘kiss the grain’ are harder to make sense of than the text they replace. Jerome himself, who translated ‘worship purely’, argued that ‘son’ was also a legitimate sense.

The disagreement is real, and English Bibles will go on differing. What the options share matters more than what divides them: every reading calls the rulers of the earth to an act of submission to God's rule through his king, and every reading ends with the same blessing on those who take refuge.

hard.q: “Today I have become Your Father”: does verse 7 make the king divine, or make Jesus a Son by adoption?
hard.a:
Two objections press from opposite directions. Jewish interpreters, from Rashi onward, read the sonship of verse 7 as the ordinary covenant status of David's heir, who is God's son in the sense of 2 Samuel 7:14 and nothing more, and they regard the Christian use of the verse for a divine Son as reading into it what is not there. Many critical scholars agree on the psalm's original meaning: Adela Yarbro Collins and John J. Collins (King and Messiah as Son of God, 2008) set the verse within ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, where kings were called sons of gods, and argue that Israel's version was an adoption on the day of enthronement. From the other side, some early Christians did read the verse as adoption. Codex Bezae and some early writers give the words at Jesus' baptism as ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you’ (Luke 3:22), and groups later called adoptionists held that Jesus became God's Son at his baptism. If the verse describes a man who becomes a son on a particular day, how can the church use it of the eternal Son?

Responses begin with the New Testament itself, which does not use verse 7 for the incarnation or for eternity. Paul applies ‘today’ to the resurrection (Acts 13:33), and Romans 1:4 speaks of Jesus being declared Son of God with power by his resurrection, language that describes the enthronement of one who was already the Son, as Romans 1:3 makes clear. Hebrews uses the verse beside texts that speak of the Son's role in creation (Hebrews 1:2-3, 1:10). Calvin argued that ‘begotten’ in the psalm means ‘made known’, the day the king's sonship was publicly declared. Augustine, followed by much of the Western tradition, read ‘today’ as God's eternal present, so that the verse speaks of eternal generation; many modern interpreters, while respecting that reading, think it goes beyond the psalm's plain sense. The church's confession that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father (Nicaea, 325; Constantinople, 381) rests on the whole witness of the New Testament, especially John 1, rather than on this verse alone. Jewish readers and Christians can agree that the psalm first described a royal adoption. Christians confess that the one who fulfilled it was no mere adopted king but the eternal Son who, as a son of David, was enthroned at his resurrection.

observe: The psalm has four stanzas with four different speakers. Who speaks in verses 1 to 3, 4 to 6, 7 to 9, and 10 to 12, and what does each say?
What exactly do the rulers want to break and cast away in verse 3, and whose ‘chains’ and ‘cords’ are they?
List the commands given to the kings in verses 10 to 12. What promise closes the psalm?
interpret: The same verb describes the righteous man meditating in Psalm 1:2 and the nations plotting in Psalm 2:1. What does the pairing of these two psalms at the start of the Psalter suggest about how to read the whole book?

The church in Acts 4 applied verses 1 and 2 to Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel. Why is it significant that they saw the psalm fulfilled first in the cross rather than in a Christian victory?
Paul applies verse 7 to the resurrection (Acts 13:33). In what sense was Easter a day of enthronement?
apply: Where do you experience God's authority as chains to be thrown off, and what would it look like to see it instead as the rule of a King who offers refuge?
God's laughter in verse 4 is not anxiety. How might that change the way you respond to news about powerful people and nations?
The psalm warns rulers but ends with an invitation. How can you speak to people with power over you, or under you, with both warning and welcome?
